title: Clustered Attractor Manifolds and Dynamical Condensation in Self-Attention
authors: Qucheng Gao, Zuyi Yang, Xiao Chen
abstract: Transformer layers generate state-dependent interaction networks: token representations determine the attention matrix, which in turn updates the representations. We study this feedback in a minimal normalized self-attention dynamics and identify the overlap gap as the central quantity governing its attractor structure in the thermodynamic limit. When tokens form internally aligned clusters and their similarity to members of the same cluster exceeds that to every other cluster by a nonvanishing amount, inter-cluster attention is exponentially suppressed as the dimension increases. This mechanism produces a high-dimensional manifold of clustered fixed points, ranging from a few macroscopic clusters to extensive microscopic fragmentation, and also controls their stability against perturbations. Starting from an unstructured Gaussian state, we find that clustered states nucleate from the diffuse background only above a finite threshold in attention sharpness, giving rise to a dynamical attention-condensation transition.
summary: This paper analyzes self-attention mechanisms by mapping them onto a statistical mechanics model to understand their dynamic attractors. It identifies that attention condensation occurs above a critical sharpness threshold ($ eta$), leading to stable, clustered fixed points characterized by an overlap gap. The work provides theoretical insights into how information processing in Transformers transitions between diffuse and highly structured collective states.
main_problem: The study investigates the attractor structure, stability, and phase transitions of self-attention dynamics within Transformer layers by treating token interactions as a statistical mechanics problem.
main_result: The system exhibits a dynamical attention-condensation transition above a finite threshold in attention sharpness ($ eta$), leading to stable clustered fixed points characterized by an overlap gap ($\Delta > 0$).
method: The analysis employs mean-field approximations, studies the dynamics in the thermodynamic limit ($d \sim N 	o \infty$), and analyzes scaling laws for various observables.
model_or_system: The model is minimal normalized self-attention dynamics applied to $N$ token vectors $\mathbf{x}_i(t)$, governed by an iterative update rule dependent on the attention matrix derived from overlaps. The system transitions between diffuse, macroscopic clustered, and fragmented states.
key_observables: Overlap Gap ($\Delta_a$), Attention Inverse Participation Ratios ($Y_A$, $V/N$), Effective Rank ($	ext{Reff}/N$), Largest Cluster Size ($m_{\max}/N$).
important_parameters: Attention sharpness ($ eta$), System size ($N$), Overlap gap ($\Delta$), Time ($t$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies heavily on taking the thermodynamic limit ($d \sim N 	o \infty$) for stability proofs, and uses mean-field approximations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate noise-induced fragmentation scaling with $\alpha =  eta\epsilon^2$, map out three dynamical regimes (diffuse, condensed, fragmented) vs. $ eta$, and show time evolution plateaus at $T=N$ for Gaussian initializations.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by defining the self-attention dynamics as a statistical mechanics problem, identifying key diagnostics like the overlap gap, analyzing the transition from diffuse to clustered states via condensation thresholds, and finally characterizing the stability and time evolution of these different attractor regimes.
why_interesting: The framework connects concepts from condensed matter physics (phase transitions, order parameters) directly to the dynamics of large-scale neural network models, offering insights into emergent collective behavior in deep learning architectures.
